The udu is a composite instrument of the Igbo people of Nigeria, partaking of both implosive aerophones and idiophones, with the Hornbostel-Sachs number 111.24+413.2. In Igbo, ùdù means pot, and the form comes from a water jar with an extra hole; it is usually made of clay and can also be plastic or glass, with modern versions in wood, synthetic fibreglass and other materials. To play it you rest it on your lap or tape it to a stand, strike the large hole quickly with the palm for a bass note, then cover the small hole at the top with the hand to change the pitch, and you can also tap the body with the fingers. Traditionally it was mostly played by Igbo women in rites and celebrations.
巫毒鼓源自奈及利亞伊博族，早期為多一孔的水罐，由女性在儀式中演奏，兼具內爆式氣鳴: The udu comes from the Igbo people of Nigeria: originally a water jar with an extra hole, played by women in rituals, partaking of both implosive aerophone and idiophone. Igbo tradition holds that pottery can communicate with the ancestors, and pot-making was mostly women's work. Pots were widespread because they mattered in daily life and in the economy, and their standing fell once plastic goods arrived. As the instrument spread and was remade in different places it grew from the pot shape into flat and double-chambered forms, and its materials widened to wood, synthetic fibreglass and more. The American artist Frank Giorgni devised modern types such as the Utar and Udongo, and the Persian percussionist Behnam Samani added holes and a drumhead and named it the Zarbang Udoo.
演奏時可將巫毒鼓置於膝上，或以膠帶固定在支架上。初學先以手掌快速擊打較大孔洞，取: You can rest the udu on your lap or tape it to a stand. A beginner starts by striking the larger hole quickly with the palm to get the bass, then covers the smaller hole at the top with the hand to adjust the pitch. The fingers can also tap the body for other timbres. In practice you need to keep the shape of the hand and the position of the covering hand steady, or you cannot control the changes of pitch.
烏杜鼓擁有深沉、溫潤的音色質感，帶有獨特的陶土共鳴特徵。其音域較低，以中低頻為主: The udu has a deep, warm timbre with the particular resonance of fired clay. Its range is low, mostly in the low and middle frequencies, with rich harmonic content. When the palm strikes the opening the sound is warm and full yet carries light high overtones, a distinctive contrast. The resonance of the chamber gives the sound a floating, spatial quality: it is neither as bright and sharp as a drumhead nor as dull and heavy as a bass drum. Compared with African drums, the udu is softer and more inward; compared with Western percussion its sound has more of a raw, ethnic flavour, with the warm tone that belongs to clay instruments, and it can create a mysterious, quicksilver atmosphere.
